artifacts.summary: 5-phase implementation: pending_dispatch pre-image capture, orchestrate-unwind-dispatch.sh recovery script, integration fixture test, documentation, shellcheck/redeploy verification.

completion_data.completion_summary: Added orchestrate-unwind-dispatch.sh, the sanctioned by-hand recovery path for a /orchestrate dispatch prepared but never issued: it restores state.json status/last_updated/session_id, the durable dispatch_seq_counter, releases the lock, deletes the dispatch file, and clears pending_dispatch, or refuses cleanly. Widened orchestrate-cycle-plan.sh's pending_dispatch record with the prior_* pre-image the recovery script needs, documented the script across the state-machine doc, git-safety.md, and SKILL.md, and verified with a real end-to-end fixture test, shellcheck, and a clean redeploy.

memory_candidates.content: When a durable per-task guard file (e.g. .orchestrator-loop-guard) needs a 'prior value' pre-image captured before this run's own writes, capture it at the EARLIEST point the script already reads that file this invocation -- not immediately before the write site that will use it. An intervening flush for the SAME key elsewhere in the same script run (e.g. an aux-dispatch-emission loop that runs between the seed loop and the main per-task loop) can corrupt a late re-read into recording the just-written value as if it were the original.

A recovery/undo script that must release a lock 'only if this session holds it' should delegate that check to the existing acquire/release helper's own built-in holder-identity comparison (e.g. task-lock.sh release already WARNs and no-ops on a session mismatch) rather than re-implementing a parallel check-then-release sequence. Fewer duplicated identity checks means one less place for the two copies to drift out of sync.

For a fixture test proving a new script correctly reverses another script's mutations, prefer running the REAL upstream script to prepare fixture state over hand-constructing the intermediate JSON by hand. A hand-built fixture can pass even when the two scripts' actual field-population contract has drifted; running the real upstream script end-to-end catches that class of bug (caught here: the fixture's first draft used the wrong CLI invocation for the upstream script, which only surfaced because it was actually invoked rather than assumed).
